In mathematics, an '''EP matrix''' (or '''range-Hermitian matrix'''<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Drivaliaris|first=Dimosthenis|last2=Karanasios|first2=Sotirios|last3=Pappas|first3=Dimitrios|date=2008-10-01|title=Factorizations of EP operators|journal=Linear Algebra and Its Applications|volume=429|issue=7|pages=1555–1567|doi=10.1016/j.laa.2008.04.026|issn=0024-3795|arxiv=0806.2088}}</ref> or '''RPN matrix'''<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|title=Matrix analysis and applied linear algebra|last=Meyer|first=Carl D.|date=2000|publisher=Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics|isbn=0898714540|location=Philadelphia|oclc=43662189}}</ref>) is a square matrix ''A'' whose range is equal to the range of its [[conjugate transpose]] ''A''*. Another equivalent characterization of EP matrices is that the range of ''A'' is orthogonal to the nullspace of ''A''. Thus, EP matrices are also known as RPN (Range Perpendicular to Nullspace) matrices.   

EP matrices were introduced in 1950 by [[Hans Schwerdtfeger]],<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite book|title=Introduction to linear algebra and the theory of matrices|last=Schwerdtfeger|first=Hans|publisher=P. Noordhoff|year=1950}}</ref> and since then, many equivalent characterizations of EP matrices have been investigated through the literature.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Cheng|first=Shizhen|last2=Tian|first2=Yongge|date=2003-12-01|title=Two sets of new characterizations for normal and EP matrices|journal=Linear Algebra and Its Applications|volume=375|pages=181–195|doi=10.1016/S0024-3795(03)00650-5|issn=0024-3795|doi-access=free}}</ref> The meaning of the EP abbreviation stands originally for ''E''qual ''P''rincipal, but it is widely believed that it stands for ''Equal [[Projection (linear algebra)|Projectors]]'' instead, since an equivalent characterization of EP matrices is based in terms of equality of the projectors ''AA<sup>+</sup>'' and ''A<sup>+</sup>A''.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Scalar, Vector, and Matrix Mathematics : Theory, Facts, and Formulas.|last=S.|first=Bernstein, Dennis|date=2018|publisher=Princeton University Press|isbn=9781400888252|location=Princeton|oclc=1023540775}}</ref>

The range of any matrix ''A'' is perpendicular to the null-space of ''A''*, but is not necessarily perpendicular to the null-space of ''A''. When ''A'' is an EP matrix, the range of ''A'' is precisely perpendicular to the null-space of ''A''.

== Properties ==
* An equivalent characterization of an EP matrix ''A'' is that ''A'' commutes with its [[Moore-Penrose inverse]], that is, the projectors ''AA<sup>+</sup>'' and ''A<sup>+</sup>A'' are equal. This is similar to the characterization of normal matrices where ''A'' commutes with its conjugate transpose.<ref name=":1" /> As a corollary, [[nonsingular matrix|nonsingular matrices]] are always EP matrices.

* The sum of EP matrices ''A''<sub>i</sub> is an EP matrix if the null-space of the sum is contained in the null-space of each matrix ''A''<sub>i</sub>.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Meenakshi|first=A.R.|date=1983|title=On sums of EP matrices|journal=Houston Journal of Mathematics|volume=9|citeseerx=10.1.1.638.7389}}</ref>
* To be an EP matrix is a necessary condition for normality: ''A'' is normal if and only if ''A'' is EP matrix and ''AA''*''A''<sup>2</sup> = ''A''<sup>2</sup>''A''*''A''.<ref name=":1" />
* When ''A'' is an EP matrix, the Moore-Penrose inverse of ''A'' is equal to the [[Drazin inverse|group inverse]] of ''A''.<ref name=":1" />
* ''A'' is an EP matrix if and only if the Moore-Penrose inverse of ''A'' is an EP matrix.<ref name=":1" />

== Decomposition ==
The [[spectral theorem]] states that a matrix is normal if and only if it is [[Similar matrix|unitarily similar]] to a [[diagonal matrix]]. 

Weakening the normality condition to EPness, a similar statement is still valid. Precisely, a matrix ''A'' of rank ''r'' is an EP matrix if and only if it is unitarily similar to a core-nilpotent matrix,<ref name=":2" /> that is,

: <math>A = U \begin{pmatrix} C & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} U^{*},</math>

where ''U'' is an [[orthogonal matrix]] and ''C'' is an ''r'' x ''r'' nonsingular matrix. Note that if ''A'' is full rank, then ''A'' = ''UCU''<sup>*</sup>.
